name: point-to-point-channel
intent: Deliver each message on a channel to exactly one consumer, so senders never have to coordinate with receivers and no unit of work is handled twice.
problem: A producer must hand work to exactly one handler while several receivers are running (or the intended handler is temporarily unavailable): broadcasting the message makes every receiver deduplicate, and addressing a specific consumer instance couples the sender to its identity, location and liveness.
context: Asynchronous messaging inside one process, between processes or across services, where each message is a unit of work (command, job, document, RPC request) and duplicate handling is as unacceptable as loss. Applies to in-process worker queues and to brokered channels (JMS queue, AMQP queue, Kafka partition, cloud queue) alike; the channel - not the consumer and not the sender - owns the routing decision.
benefits: Removes receiver coordination: the channel picks the consumer, so several workers share the load without locks, leader election or a dispatcher component.
Decouples the sender from receiver identity, location and liveness: a sender names only the channel, while consumers may restart, scale or move independently.
Makes the delivery contract explicit and testable: 'exactly one consumer per message' is a property of the channel instead of a convention every handler must honour.
Enables load levelling and backpressure: a bounded or broker-held queue absorbs bursts and consumers pull at the rate they can sustain.
Composes with reliability tooling: acknowledgement, redelivery, dead-lettering and depth monitoring attach to the channel rather than to each consumer.
tradeoffs: The channel is a serialization point: a single hot queue caps throughput at the broker or lock even as consumers are added, and ordering guarantees vanish once several consumers compete.
Point-to-point is an implicit one-consumer assumption: attaching a second logical consumer by mistake silently steals messages instead of informing both.
At-least-once delivery across failures reopens the duplicate window: without idempotent receivers or transactional consumption, 'exactly one' degrades to 'at least one, possibly twice'.
In-process queues lose buffered messages when the process dies, and every implementation invents its own shutdown story (poison pills, closed flags, interrupted blocking reads).
Unbounded queues turn overload into memory growth or an ever-growing backlog, while bounded queues turn it into producer blocking or dropped messages - one of the two must be chosen explicitly.

participants.responsibility: Creates a message and writes it to the channel; knows the channel identity, never which consumer will handle it.
Owns the delivery contract: buffers messages and hands each one to exactly one receiver, blocking or rejecting the sender when its bound is reached.
Takes messages from the channel and processes them; several consumers may be attached, but any single message reaches only one of them.
The unit of work in transit, carrying an identity and headers that survive redelivery so duplicate detection, correlation and tracing are possible.
Persists the queue, tracks acknowledgements and redelivery, and enforces the one-consumer rule for remote participants.

use_cases: Work queues: a web tier enqueues jobs and a pool of workers consumes them, with each job running exactly once.
Request-reply over messaging: the request goes to a queue, exactly one service instance answers it, and the reply returns on a reply queue identified by a correlation identifier.
Command dispatch in a service-oriented system: an order service appends commands that exactly one instance of the command processor executes.
Media or log processing pipelines where every stage pulls its input from a queue and each item is handled by one of the stage's replicas.
Legacy and batch integration: jobs handed to a single consumer daemon through a queue, with the channel providing the transactional hand-off.
Scaling an existing single-consumer endpoint by attaching additional instances (Competing Consumers) without changing producers or the message contract.
Apache Kafka consumer groups: records in each topic partition are assigned to one group member at a time, so a group scales work while separate group IDs retain independent pub-sub copies.

RabbitMQ Work Queues: a task queue distributes jobs among competing workers with round-robin or fair dispatch; manual acknowledgements allow unacknowledged work to be redelivered after a worker failure.

Amazon SQS Standard queues: distribute background jobs among consumers with visibility timeouts, while at-least-once delivery requires idempotent handlers because duplicate deliveries remain possible.
avoid_when: Every interested receiver must see the message: that is a publish-subscribe channel or an event topic, not a queue.
The payload is a domain event with several independent subscribers; model the subscribers explicitly instead of stealing messages from a queue.
A single in-process consumer with no scaling, durability or cross-process requirement: a direct call, a lock-protected collection or a plain task queue is simpler.
Strict ordering per key is required while consumers scale: partition the channel by key (or use a datatype channel per key) rather than sharing one queue.
The interaction is a synchronous call expecting an immediate answer: a direct request-response API avoids queue latency and correlation plumbing.
anti_patterns: Attaching a second logical consumer (for example an audit listener) to a point-to-point channel, silently stealing half the messages instead of receiving copies - use a wire tap or a pub-sub channel.
Using a point-to-point channel for event notification to several independent subsystems and then discovering that only one of them ever runs.
Unbounded in-memory queues as an architecture: overload becomes memory growth and buffered work disappears on restart.
Non-idempotent consumers on an at-least-once channel: redelivery after a failure repeats side effects such as charging a card twice.
A hand-rolled 'queue' as a list polled from a timer callback without synchronization, which duplicates and loses messages under load.
design_principles: Separation of concerns: the routing decision (which consumer receives a message) lives in the channel, not in senders or consumers.
Single responsibility: producers produce, consumers consume, the channel delivers.
Information hiding: the sender knows the channel identity only, never the set or number of consumers.
Open/closed principle: consumer count and capacity change without touching producer or consumer code.
Explicit contracts: the delivery guarantee (at-most-once vs at-least-once) is documented at the channel because consumers must be written against it.
best_practices: State the delivery guarantee explicitly and make consumers idempotent whenever at-least-once semantics are possible.
Bound the queue and decide the overflow policy (block the producer, shed load, spill to disk) instead of letting growth be accidental.
Start with one consumer per channel and add competitors only together with idempotency and tolerance for out-of-order processing.
Give messages identity, timestamps and a correlation identifier so duplicates, redeliveries and poison messages are diagnosable.
Define an end-of-stream marker or close operation and drain in-flight messages before shutting consumers down.
Monitor queue depth, consumer lag and the age of the oldest message; they are the leading indicators of consumer starvation.
sources: Hohpe & Woolf, Enterprise Integration Patterns: Designing, Building, and Deploying Messaging Solutions (2003) - Point-to-Point Channel (Messaging Channels chapter).
